definition: How low or high a sound is, in hertz (Hz). 1 kHz = 1,000 Hz. Humans hear about 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
The lowest frequency of a note, which sets its pitch. A low E on bass is about 41 Hz.
Higher frequencies above the fundamental that give a sound its character.
How much a band turns up (+) or down (−), in decibels.
A unit of loudness change. About 1 dB is the smallest change most people notice; 6 dB is a big one.
How wide a band is. Low Q is broad, high Q is narrow.
A band shaped like a hill or valley around one frequency.
Raises or lowers everything above (high shelf) or below (low shelf) a frequency.
Removes everything below or above a frequency. Also called high-pass / low-pass.
How steeply a cut falls off, in dB per octave. 12 is gentle, 48 is steep.
A doubling of frequency: 100 Hz to 200 Hz is one octave.
A very narrow, deep cut for one frequency.
Brightens or darkens the whole sound around one point.
A frequency that rings louder than its neighbors.
Too much energy in the low mids (about 200–500 Hz), making a mix cloudy.
Sharp S, T, and SH sounds in a voice, around 5–9 kHz.
An EQ band that only moves when the sound crosses a threshold.
The level where a dynamic band starts acting.
The most a dynamic band can cut (−) or boost (+).
How quickly a dynamic band reaches its range once past threshold.
How gently the band starts moving near the threshold.
How fast a dynamic band reacts.
How fast a dynamic band lets go.
The share of the last 10 seconds a dynamic band spent moving.
The part of a dynamic band that listens and decides when to move.
Letting another track control this one. Set it in Logic's Side Chain menu.
Lets dynamic bands react a moment early, by delaying the audio slightly.
Mid is the center of a stereo sound; Side is the difference between left and right.
The timing of a wave. EQs shift it slightly near the frequencies they change.
An EQ mode that keeps all frequencies in time, at the cost of delay.
A faint swell before sharp hits, caused by linear-phase EQ.
Delay added by processing. Logic compensates for it during playback.
A loudness measurement close to how loud people hear a song.
Keeps the output level matched to the input so EQ changes are judged fairly.
Plays only what the EQ is adding or removing.
The space between your loudest peak and 0 dBFS, where clipping starts.
The moving graph that shows how much energy is at each frequency.
A finished song you compare your mix against.
